quickStart.title: Quick Start
quickStart.description: Add MCP Moira to your AI assistant. Choose your client below:

claude-web.description:
1. Go to claude.ai → Settings → Connectors
2. Click "Add custom connector"
3. Enter server URL and click "Connect"
4. Complete OAuth in browser

Requires Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise plan.

chatgpt.description:
1. Go to chat.openai.com → Settings → Connectors
2. Click "Add connector"
3. Enter name "MCP Moira" and server URL
4. Complete OAuth authentication

Requires Plus or Pro plan.

claude-code.authIntro: Then authenticate with your MCP Moira account:
claude-code.authContent:
Browser will open for OAuth authentication.
Authorize and return to terminal.

claude-desktop.description:
1. Open Settings (⌘+,) → Connectors tab
2. Click "Add custom connector"
3. Enter server URL and click "Connect"
4. Browser opens for OAuth → Done

No config file editing needed.

cursor.authIntro: Then authenticate with your MCP Moira account:
cursor.authContent:
Browser will open for OAuth authentication.
Authorize and return to Cursor.

vscode.authIntro: Then authenticate with your MCP Moira account:
vscode.authContent:
Browser will open for OAuth authentication.
Authorize and return to VS Code.

perplexity.description:
1. Install PerplexityXPC helper (Settings → Connectors → Install Helper)
2. Click "Add Connector"
3. Enter server name and MCP command
4. Complete OAuth authentication

Paid plan recommended. Uses mcp-remote bridge.

copilot-cli.authIntro: After saving the config file, authenticate:
copilot-cli.authContent:
1. Start a Copilot CLI session
2. Type /mcp
3. Select "moira" → Authenticate
→ Browser opens for OAuth

variables.guideBody: Every value here comes from the run's route: the variables the workflow declares and the fields each step returned. Open a variable's history to see which step changed it and when; edit a value in its row where the run allows it. Answering the waiting step or editing a variable acts on the run, never on the definition, and is recorded in the route as an adjustment with your name on it.

process.title: This is a process
process.body: A Moira workflow is a process: a sequence of named stages a piece of work goes through. We call each stage a block. What you see highlighted is a block: it has a name, a description of what has to happen there, and arrows to the blocks it can lead to.

agent.title: An agent runs it, one step at a time
agent.body: An AI agent executes the process. Inside every block are steps: one step is one instruction Moira hands the agent, with a condition for when it counts as done. Moira gives out exactly one step at a time; the agent cannot skip ahead. The highlight is the step the agent is on right now in this run.

evidence.title: It must return evidence
evidence.body: To finish a step, the agent must return evidence: the fields the step asks for, checked against a schema before Moira lets the run continue. The highlighted list is exactly what this step demands back. No matching evidence, no next step.

loop.title: A failed review sends the work back
loop.body: Some steps are reviews. When a review finds problems, the process does not continue: it returns to an earlier block, and the work is done again. That return is a loop. The highlighted chip marks one of this process's loops: hover it to light the return arrow and read what causes it.

route.title: Every run leaves a route
route.body: A run is one execution of the process. Moira records its route: every step in order, every loop it went through, and the values the steps produced along the way. This is the route of this run; the variables tab shows its values, and any adjustment a person made is marked.

explore.title: Explore the same run your way
explore.body: The two views show the same run: the Map is the process with the run's state on it, the Graph is every node of the definition. Your selection and the graph's viewport survive a switch.

map.title: Map: the process as a diagram
map.body: Blocks are laid out left to right in process order; thin dashed lines below are loops. Every loop, skip and exit into a shared block is named by a chip in its source block; hover the chip (or the line) to light it and read its label, and select a block to keep its lines lit. A card carries the block's run state: how many times it ran, how long its passes took and, when the block works through a list, how much of that list is done. The contents on the left jump to any block and the finder there answers "which block is this step in". The map opens on the block the run is at.

flowPage.title: Flow
flowPage.noProcess: This workflow declares no process view (no blocks), so the page shows its node graph. Add a `progress` section with blocks to read it as a process.

map.title: Map: the process as a diagram
map.body: Blocks are laid out left to right in process order; thin dashed lines below are loops. Every loop, skip and exit into a shared block is named by a chip in its source block; hover the chip (or the line) to light it and read its label, and select a block to keep its lines lit. The contents on the left jump to any block and the finder there answers "which block is this step in"; the panel on the right holds the block's description, its steps and, in edit mode, the authoring controls.

registry.guideBody: Every global variable the workflow declares, with its type, description and default. Steps read them by name in their directives and conditions; a run's values appear on the run page. Undeclared names cannot be used.

registry.title: Declared variables

edit.hint: Edit mode changes the workflow definition itself — block names and descriptions, transition labels and loop explanations, which block a step belongs to, a step's directive or expressions, and the variable registry. It never touches a run. Edits live on the page until you save them; the save is refused if someone else changed the workflow in the meantime.
edit.guideTitle: You are editing the process definition
edit.guideBody: Change a block's name or description in place; click the pencil next to a transition to change its label or its loop's cause and exit; in the block panel, move a step to another block or edit its text; in Variables, edit the registry. Both views re-derive at once, rule violations appear as diagnostics, "Export" lists exactly which flow-file entries would change, and "Save" sends the definition to the server against the revision you loaded.
edit.conflict: Someone changed this workflow since you loaded it. Reload the page and apply your edits again.
edit.exportHint: Path in the workflow JSON, value before, value after — exactly what the save sends.
edit.label: Label

process.title: This is a process
process.body: A Moira workflow is a process: a sequence of named stages a piece of work goes through. We call each stage a block. What you see highlighted is a block: it has a name, a description of what has to happen there, and arrows to the blocks it can lead to.

agent.title: An agent runs it, one step at a time
agent.body: An AI agent executes the process. Inside every block are steps: one step is one instruction Moira hands the agent, with a condition for when it counts as done. Moira gives out exactly one step at a time; the agent cannot skip ahead. The highlight is one step of this block.

evidence.title: It must return evidence
evidence.body: To finish a step, the agent must return evidence: the fields the step asks for, checked against a schema before Moira lets the run continue. The highlighted list is exactly what this step demands back. No matching evidence, no next step.

loop.title: A failed review sends the work back
loop.body: Some steps are reviews. When a review finds problems, the process does not continue: it returns to an earlier block, and the work is done again. That return is a loop. The highlighted chip marks one of this process's loops: hover it to light the return arrow and read what causes it and what ends it.

edit.title: The definition can be edited here
edit.body: This page shows the definition, not a run. Its owner can turn on edit mode to change block names and descriptions, transition labels, which block a step belongs to, a step's text and the variable registry; the views update at once and the save is checked by the server. Runs of this workflow are read on the run page.
